CNBC, 18 Nov 2026 17:08 GMT

The short end of the Treasury yield curve was relatively unchanged on Wednesday after Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller called for aggressive action against inflation, which he said has been more persistent than he expected.

Later in the day the Street will read the latest FOMC minutes from the central bank's October meeting for potential insight into Fed officials' thinking on the path of interest rates.

The 2-year Treasury yield, which reacts most to changes in expectations of Fed policy, was last trading down less than 1 basis point to 4.783% after shooting up more than 4 basis points to 4.83% earlier in the day. The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield lost more than 3 basis points to 5.064%, while the long-dated 30-year Treasury bond yield was down more than 4 basis points at 5.414%.

One basis point equals 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.

Waller jolted the market Wednesday by telling CNBC in a live interview that a half-percentage-point increase in the Fed's benchmark rate is probably necessary at the Dec. 8-9 meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee.

From here, Waller said the Fed needs to reverse the three quarter-point reductions from last year and may need to do more.

"You might need to, like, shock people," Waller told CNBC's Steve Liesman during the "Squawk Box" interview.

"I'm very, very concerned about inflation. It's kind of headed in the wrong direction, and it's spreading out," he said. "If you really want to get it down, you've got to start taking more aggressive actions."

Traders have now priced in a 95% chance of a quarter-percentage-point rate hike, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool.

At the same time, FOMC minutes from the Fed's Oct. 27–28 meeting, which saw policymakers hold rates at 3.75%–4% in a 10–2 vote, are due later in the session. Fed governors Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack were the dissenters, calling for a quarter-point hike.

October U.S. retail sales came in stronger than expected on Tuesday, potentially strengthening the case for further interest rate hikes. Stripping out volatile gas and auto data, retail sales were up 0.6% and higher than expectations of 0.4%.

— With additional reporting by CNBC's Jeff Cox
